title: The Era of Cognitive Automation (fivetwelvethirteen.substack.com), September 1, 2026
author: Dylan Kane
source: Five Twelve Thirteen (fivetwelvethirteen.substack.com), Five Twelve Thirteen
summary: Dylan Kane offers a speculative but evidence-grounded narrative to explain why student achievement, after a century of steady gains tracked by the Flynn effect, began reversing across the developed world around 2013. He argues the reversal cannot be pinned on schools, since the decline shows up simultaneously in IQ scores, cross-national achievement data, and even adult cognitive measures well outside any classroom's influence. Instead he proposes 'cognitive automation' -- calculators, television, streaming, social media, and now large language models -- as the real driver, arguing that automation has begun outstripping the complexity of the world that once forced humans to think harder. Kane is careful to distinguish this from a defense of schools, acknowledging real dysfunction in education while insisting that outside forces have had a far larger effect on learning outcomes than anything happening inside classrooms. He closes on a note of cautious optimism, urging educators to resist nostalgia and quick fixes and instead build better practice through patient, evidence-stitching work.
points: Frames the 20th-century Flynn effect (steady generational IQ gains) as evidence that a more abstract, complex world made humans measurably smarter over time, not schooling itself.

Argues the post-2013 reversal in student achievement is a global, cross-domain phenomenon -- visible in IQ tests, NAEP-style data, and adult cognitive measures -- which rules out any single national schooling failure as the cause.

Proposes 'cognitive automation' (calculators, TV, streaming, social media, LLMs) as the mechanism displacing the hard thinking that once drove cognitive gains, accelerating sharply in the last fifteen years.
Explicitly rejects both nostalgia for a supposed golden age of schooling and the impulse to blame or fully exonerate schools, insisting the evidence points mostly outside the classroom.
Calls for humble, iterative, evidence-based improvement in teaching practice rather than searching for quick fixes or trying to recreate a prior decade's conditions.
quotes: For the entirety of the 20th century, across the developed world, each generation of humans was a bit smarter than the last. The best evidence we have for this is the Flynn effect. Humans have steadily improved on IQ tests over that century, where each decade the average test-taker improved by about 3 points.
We can’t attribute much of these gains to what was happening in schools. There’s just no evidence that the quality of education has made a substantive difference.
Either there was a broad conspiracy across almost the entire developed world to ruin schools while also somehow making adults decades out of school dumber, or the cause isn’t actually in schools.

Here’s the story I’m telling. For a long time, as the world became more complex, that complexity caused humans to think harder and think more and made us smarter. Then, a second trend began: cognitive automation displaced some of that thinking, slowly at first but then faster and faster.
I’m not saying school is useless. If school disappeared tomorrow, student achievement would plummet. Covid was an unfortunate but illustrative natural experiment to prove that point.
Horace complained over two thousand years ago about kids these days, and we haven’t stopped since. Every generation has argued that we are declining from some golden age in the past.
We won’t build a better education system by looking to the past. It will be something built, brick by brick, by humble, knowledgeable, passionate, and persistent educators.
